chapter: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
title: Traditional players pushed out and black audiences leaving at a two-beat
summary: Hodes laments the clarinetists thrown away by the press and Big Bill Broonzy booed by his own people. He recalls Chicago black audiences leaving when he played two-beat but staying for ballads.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: From the press people, yeah. Because your heart is where your money is, and they're making their living there. And so there seems to be a separation now. There's a coolness that's coming. But more than that, think of the tragedy of the great clarinetists, Jimmy Noone, who never made number one on the poll.

They become thrown in the ashcan. That's the whole style. And ten years of their lives is taken away from them, because if you don't work, if you -- did you ever read the liner notes that Studs Terkel wrote for Columbia Artists on Big Bill Broonzy's appearance in Niagara or some town? Studs loaned it to me. He's booed by his own people, he's booed out, because of the music. He's old-fashioned, he's old hat.

I worked the Capital Lounge in Chicago, and I got what we call a Dixieland setup, clarinet, trombone and trumpet. But I got Buddy Smith on drums. Buddy has played with Diz, he's played with the Bird, he's played with Zut and now he's playing with me. He's a good drummer.

So the audience is black. We hit a two-beat number, and the audience clears out and is in the street. And then Buddy and I do a number together, and they come back. And let me tell you another instance. I'm booked in a place called Stars of Jazz, New Stars of Jazz, in Chicago, right near the Union Station. The Rising Stars of Jazz, that's what it was.
And Lena -- what was this girl singer that come out
No, no, smaller name. But, no -- anyway, she has a club of her own on the South Side now.
Lurleen Hunter is playing there. Les Strand is playing piano and Parker or something like that, a big black pianist; I don't know. Anyway, he's still around playing cocktails.
Les Strand, by the way, is back in Chicago.

So there are -- this is the club and I'm booked there, playing off nights, for both the organist and the piano. I go into a two-beat number, 'Ballin' the Jack' or something, and the house started shuffling their feet, getting up, moving around. I play 'Washboard Blues' and there ain't a sound. I play any ballad and they sit there now beautiful that thing was. They don't move.

But the minute I play two-beat, out they go. And this was what has happened because of this. That's bad, but the real bad part was, like, Big Bill Broonzy and putting him out of work, and putting all these great players, take ten years out of the life. This is what I objected to, in retrospect.
